newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Gle des Eaux unveils key telecom partners.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gle des Eaux unveils key telecom partners.

text.p: French utilities group Compagnie Generale des Eaux (CGE) on Thursday unveiled its list of partners in a seven billion franc ($1.36 billion) telecommunications venture that aims to make it France's second biggest player.

CGE chairman Jean-Marie Messier said it had chosen British Telecommunications Plc as its "premier strategic partner" in the Cegetel company, which will compete against state-owned France Telecom from 1998.
The French market will open up to private operators from January 1998 under a European Union (EU) directive that ends France Telecom's domestic monopoly.
Messier told a news conference this was "the first day of competition in the French telecommunications market".
CGE will hold 50 percent of Cegetel, BT 25 percent, U.S. telecoms firm SBC 15 percent and Germany's Mannesman AG 10 percent.
But Messier said the final stakes could change by five percent either way when final contracts were signed late 1996.
The company will have seven billion francs capital to meet its investment needs over the next three years.
"Cegetel will enable us to introduce real competition and choice to the French telecommunications market across a wide range of services," BT chairman Ian Vallance said.

"We look forward to competing head-to-head with France Telecom across the full spectrum of telecommunications services, including of course the residential telephone market. The opportunity is too good ... to miss."

CGE already runs the SFR French mobile telephone network through the French Cofira consortium and has made Cegetel its vehicle to seize a share in the lucrative long-distance call and corporate network sectors.
A number of crucial corporate moves lie behind the creation of Cegetel, which Messier will chair.
CGE will transfer its SFR unit to Cegetel.
French telecommunications and engineering giant Alcatel Alsthom is selling its 25 percent stake in Cofira to BT for an undisclosed amount.
BT is paying 1.1 billion pounds ($1.71 billion) in cash for 25 percent in Cegetel and transferring its BT France subsidiary to Cegetel. Vallance declined to put a value on the French subsidiary.
SBC is investing 1.5 billion francs to raise its share in the Transcell holding company, which holds SBC's 15 percent stake in Cegetel, to 30 percent from 22 percent.
Messier declined to give details of how Mannesman was acquiring its 10 percent in Cegetel. In Germany, a Mannesman spokesman said it could raise that stake to 15 percent.
The Cegetel deal effectively sidelines a relationship CGE has with U.S. telecoms giant AT&T and the European Unisource consortium. "We had to make a choice for the partner for Cegetel," Messier said.
Through its link-up with BT, the French company will gain access to the Concert joint venture the British company created with MCI of the U.S., giving Cegetel a global stretch.

Messier said Cegetel aims to capture 40 percent of the domestic mobile telephone market by 2003, a market which is expected to grow almost tenfold. It wants 10 percent of the long-distance market and 10 percent of all local calls. ($1=.6416 Pound) ($1=5.145 French Franc)
